## Author's thesis (paraphrased from source)

The AQuA Book presents itself as guidance on "producing good quality analysis for government to support well informed decision-making that creates better outcomes and improve the lives of citizens" [V] (Ch 1, "Introduction"), and says it has made a significant contribution to cultural change in government assurance practice "by clearly setting out the core framework for assuring all forms of analytical evidence" [V] (Ch 1, "Introduction"). The 2025 edition updates the 2015 book for a world in which analysis underpins almost all policy and in which analysts now use open-source software, machine learning and AI alongside spreadsheets and proprietary software. It adds guidance on multi-use models, black box systems including AI, development, maintenance and continuous review, third parties, and publishing models, and it makes the whole guide relevant to all types of analysis [AP] (Ch 1, "1.1 The updated version (2025)").

Its argument rests on a small set of principles. No single piece of guidance can say definitively whether analysis is good enough for its purpose; instead, assurance effort should be proportionate to the risk of the intended use and the complexity of the method, should run through the whole life cycle, should cover both verification (error-free and to specification) and validation (fit for the purpose it is used for), and should accept that uncertainty is inherent in every input and output [AR] (Ch 1, "Principles of analytical quality assurance"; "1.3.1 Proportionate assurance" to "1.3.4 Uncertainty"). The mnemonic RIGOUR (Repeatable, Independent, Grounded in reality, Objective, Uncertainty-managed, Robust) gives analysts questions to ask of their own work at every stage [AP] (Ch 1, "1.3.5 Analysis with RIGOUR").

The book turns those principles into a few hard requirements and a structure of roles and stages. All analysis shall be assured, the assurer and the analyst shall be independent, and the level of assurance should be guided by a structured assessment of business risk, understood as the potential effect of an error combined with its likelihood [AR] (Ch 3, "Proportionality"; "3.2 Structured assessment of business risk and complexity"). Four roles (commissioner, analyst, assurer, approver) carry responsibilities through four life-cycle stages (engagement and scoping, design, analysis, and delivery, communication and sign-off), with proportionality considered at every stage and the cycle often iterative rather than linear [AR] (Ch 5, "5.1 Roles and responsibilities"; "5.2 The analytical lifecycle"; "5.3 Maintenance and continuous review").

Around that structure the book argues that a strong quality assurance culture, led and resourced by senior leaders, open about errors and transparent with the public, is vital for robust, high-quality analysis [AR] (Ch 4, "Quality assurance culture"; "4.1 Leadership"; Ch 9, "9.7 Analytical transparency"). Throughout, it uses "shall", "should" and "may" in senses it defines itself and calls consistent with the UK Government Functional Standards: a mandatory requirement, a comply-or-explain recommendation, and an option [AP] (Ch 1, "1.3 How to use this book").

## Part I: Purpose, provenance and how to read the book

### Origin and the revised edition

The original book was compiled by the Quality Assurance Working Group set up after Sir Nicholas Macpherson's review of modelling in government [AP] ("Acknowledgements"). The last version was published in 2015, following Macpherson's *Review of quality assurance of government models*; since then, the book says, assurance "has become part of the fabric of good practice for developing evidence to support policy development, implementation and operational excellence" [V] (Ch 1, "1.1 The updated version (2025)"). The book records that working practices have changed: the dominant tools when the last edition was written "were spreadsheets and proprietary software", and the range of methods now includes "open-source software, machine learning and Artificial Intelligence (AI)" [V] (Ch 1, "1.1 The updated version (2025)").

Based on user feedback, the new edition adds guidance on multi-use models ("large models used for many purposes with many stakeholders"), on assuring black box systems ("defined by their inputs and outputs, without insight into internal workings"), including AI, on development, maintenance and continuous review, on working with third parties such as contractors and academic groups, and on publishing models [V] (Ch 1, "1.1 The updated version (2025)"). It also gives improved guidance on what a proportionate approach to assurance means and makes the whole guide relevant to all types of analysis [AP] (Ch 1, "1.1 The updated version (2025)").

### Standing among other government guidance

The book calls itself "a vital supporting guide for the Analysis Function Standard" [V], and reports that the Standard refers to it extensively and notes that the "detailed guidance on the analytical cycle and management of analysis included in the Aqua Book should be followed" [V] [BT] (Ch 1, "1.1 The updated version (2025)"). It is also referred to by the Green Book, the Magenta Book, other Functional Standards such as the Finance Function Standards, the Duck Book for Code Quality Assurance, and the National Audit Office's *Quality assurance of models: a guide for audit committees* [BT] (Ch 1, "1.1 The updated version (2025)").

### Audience

The edition "has been developed for Government Analysis and is intended for anyone who commissions, uses, conducts, or assures analysis" [V]. "While it is designed with government needs in mind, the guidance is broadly applicable." [V] It covers the full process of producing analysis that is robust, reliable and fit for purpose, and it names users of commissioned analysis and senior leaders with an interest in analytical assurance among those it can help [AP] (Ch 1, "1.2 Who the AQuA Book is for"). The professions it lists are actuaries, data scientists, economists, finance professionals, geographers, operational researchers, science and engineering professionals, social researchers and statisticians [AP] (Ch 1, "1.2 Who the AQuA Book is for").

### What the book is meant to help with

The book lists six aims for the analysis community: publishing insights used for major decisions and operations; minimising "the risk of errors arising that cause operational, business or reputational damage" [V]; creating greater trust in analysts' work; ensuring appropriate quality assurance to manage mistakes, handle changing requirements and ensure appropriate re-use; developing the confidence needed for transparency and public openness; and supporting the analytical assurance required for audit purposes, with a pointer to *Managing public money* Annex 4.2, Use of models [AP] (Ch 1, "1.3 How to use this book").

### Reading order and the life-cycle picture

The first four chapters cover definitions and themes, and the second half goes into detail on the analytical life cycle [AP] (Ch 1, "1.3 How to use this book"). The life-cycle diagram is described in the text as a flowchart of four main stages, Engagement and Scoping (Chapter 6), Design (Chapter 7), Analysis (Chapter 8) and Delivery and Communication (Chapter 9), and as emphasising that "The process is often iterative, meaning stages may repeat or happen out of order" [V] and that proportionality (Chapter 3) "should be considered at every stage" [V] (Ch 1, "1.3 How to use this book"). The SVG itself places the four stages at the top, right, bottom and left of the diagram, carries "Start" and "Sign-off" labels at its upper left, and carries a centre note that in practice the cycle is often iterative and projects may include each phase several times, possibly out of order, with a corner note that proportionality (Chapter 3) should be considered in every phase [AP] (SVG label, `analytical_lifecycle_diagram.svg`).

### Shall, should, may

The book defines its modal verbs and says this usage is consistent with the UK Government Functional Standards [AP] (Ch 1, "1.3 How to use this book"):

- "shall": "denotes a requirement, a mandatory element, which applies in all circumstances and at all times" [V];
- "should": "denotes a recommendation, an advisory element, to be met on a ‘comply or explain’ basis" [V];
- "may": "denotes approval i.e. it’s a good idea but not mandatory or advisory" [V];
- "might": "denotes a possibility" [V];
- "can": "denotes both capability and possibility" [V];
- "is/are is used for a description" [V].

This reference keeps that modal force throughout: where the source says "shall", "should", "may" or "must", so does the paraphrase.

## Part II: Principles of analytical quality assurance

### No single definitive test

"No single piece of guidance provides a definitive assessment of whether a piece of analysis is of sufficient quality for an intended purpose." [V] The book instead sets out principles that support commissioning and producing fit-for-purpose analysis [AP] (Ch 1, "Principles of analytical quality assurance").

### Proportionate assurance

"Quality assurance effort should be appropriate to the risk associated with the intended use of the analysis and the complexity of the analytical approach." [V] The risks include financial, legal, operational and reputational effects [AP] (Ch 1, "1.3.1 Proportionate assurance"). Chapter 3 develops this.

### Assurance throughout development

"Quality assurance should be considered throughout the whole life cycle of the analysis." [V] Effective communication is called crucial in understanding the problem, designing the approach, conducting the analysis and relaying the outputs [AP] (Ch 1, "1.3.2 Assurance throughout development").

### Verification and validation

> "Analytical quality assurance is more than checking that the analysis is error-free and satisfies its specification (verification). It should also include checks that the analysis is appropriate and fit for the purpose for which it is being used (validation)."
> (Ch 1, "1.3.3 Verification and validation")

Chapters 5 to 9 develop verification and validation by stage [AP] (Ch 1, "1.3.3 Verification and validation").

### Uncertainty

"It is important to accept that uncertainty is inherent in the inputs and outputs of any piece of analysis." [V] Chapters 5 to 9 cover its treatment in each phase, and the book points to the Uncertainty Toolkit for Analysts in Government [AP] [BT] (Ch 1, "1.3.4 Uncertainty").

### Analysis with RIGOUR

The book offers RIGOUR as "An acronym some users find helpful" [V]: "Throughout all the stages of an analytical project, the analyst should ask questions of their own analysis." [V] (Ch 1, "1.3.5 Analysis with RIGOUR"). The six elements, in the book's terms:

- *Repeatable.* For a process to be considered valid, the analysis might reasonably be expected to produce the same outputs for the same inputs and constraints. Because different analysts may approach a problem differently and methods may include randomised processes, exact matches are neither guaranteed nor expected; "repeatability means that if an approach is repeated the results should be as expected" [V] (Ch 1, "1.3.5 Analysis with RIGOUR").
- *Independent.* "Analysis should be (as far as possible) free of prejudice or bias." [V] Care should be taken to balance views across stakeholders and experts [AP] (Ch 1, "1.3.5 Analysis with RIGOUR").
- *Grounded in reality.* Quality analysis takes the commissioner and analyst "on a journey as views and perceptions are challenged and connections are made between the analysis and its real consequences" [V]; this guards against failing to grasp the context of the problem [AP] (Ch 1, "1.3.5 Analysis with RIGOUR").
- *Objective.* Effective engagement and suitable challenge reduce the risk of bias and let commissioner and analyst be clear about how results are interpreted [AP] (Ch 1, "1.3.5 Analysis with RIGOUR").
- *Uncertainty-managed.* "Uncertainty is identified, managed and communicated throughout the analytical process." [V] (Ch 1, "1.3.5 Analysis with RIGOUR").
- *Robust.* "Analytical results are error free in the context of residual uncertainty and accepted limitations that make sure the analysis is used appropriately." [V] (Ch 1, "1.3.5 Analysis with RIGOUR").

The design-stage assurance in Chapter 7 asks whether the analytical plan is likely to meet the principles of RIGOUR [AP] (Ch 7, "7.2 Assurance activities").

## Part III: Definitions and concepts

Chapter 2 sets out the terms used through the rest of the book [AP] (Ch 2, "Definitions and concepts").

### Analysis, assurance and assurance activities

"Analysis is the collection, manipulation and interpretation of information and data for use in decision-making." [V] Many types of analysis may form the evidence base for a decision; the book lists actuarial, data science, economic, financial, geographical, operational research, scientific, technical and engineering research, statistical and social research as types frequently met in government [AP] (Ch 2, "Analysis"). "Analytical assurance is the process and set of practices that ensure analysis is fit for purpose." [V] (Ch 2, "Assurance"). "Assurance activities are any actions carried out in order to validate and verify analysis." [V], which may include analyst testing, peer review and reconciliation of results to independent sources [AP] (Ch 2, "Assurance activities").

### AI, machine learning and black box models

AI attempts to simulate human intelligence through techniques such as machine learning, natural language processing, robotics and generative AI, and aims at tasks that typically need human intelligence; "AI models are usually considered black box models" [V], and they can be pre-trained or custom built [AP] (Ch 2, "Artificial Intelligence"). (The tape's list of such tasks reads "problem-solving, -making, and language understanding", with a word missing before "-making"; the GOV.UK HTML has the same gap.)

"Black box models’ internal workings are not visible, easily understood, or succinctly explained." [V] They take input and produce output without clarity about how the output was reached. "This also includes proprietary models with protected intellectual property." [V] AI models, including machine learning, can often be considered a type of black box model, and "Other types of black box model may arise in future." [V] (Ch 2, "Black box models").

Machine learning uses algorithms to learn from patterns in data "without needing to programme explicit business rules" [V]; some such models are white box and others are considered black box; machine learning is a subset of AI [AP] (Ch 2, "Machine Learning").

### Business critical analysis and models

Business critical analysis is analysis that has a significant influence over finance and funding or departmental operations, is necessary to the achievement of a departmental business plan, or is analysis where an error could have significant reputational, economic or legal implications [AP] (Ch 2, "Business critical analysis"). Business critical models are models that support or provide business critical analysis [AP] (Ch 2, "Business critical models").

### The documentation set

- *Specification documentation* records the initial engagements with the commissioner: the question, the context and the boundaries of the analysis. It defines the scope, gives a mechanism for agreeing constraints such as deadlines and available resources, and defines the level of assurance the commissioner requires [AP] (Ch 2, "Specification documentation").
- *Design documentation* describes the analytical plan (methodology, inputs, software) and the planned verification and validation, and gives the assurer a basis to verify whether the analysis meets the specified requirements [AP] (Ch 2, "Design documentation").
- *Assumptions log*: a register of assumptions, from the commissioner or gathered from the analysis, that have been risk assessed and signed off by an appropriate governance group or stakeholder. Assumption logs should describe each assumption, quantify its effect and reliability, set out when and why it was made, and explain who made it and who signed it off [AP] (Ch 2, "Assumptions log").
- *Decisions log*: a register of decisions, provided by the commissioner or derived from the analysis. Decisions logs should describe each decision, when and why it was made, and who made and signed it off [AP] (Ch 2, "Decisions log").
- *Data log*: a register of data provided by the commissioner or derived from the analysis that has been risk assessed and signed off by an appropriate governance group or stakeholder [AP] (Ch 2, "Data log").
- *User and technical documentation.* "All analysis shall have user documentation, even if the only user is the analyst leading the analysis." [V] It should include a summary with the context of the question, the methods considered, what analysis was planned and why, the challenges met and how they were overcome, the verification and validation performed, and whether the analysis, its data and assumptions have a defined lifespan or depend on conditions to remain valid. The analyst may include a model map of data flows and transformations. Analysis likely to be revisited should have more comprehensive documentation for a future analyst, and it may help to include guidance on what should be considered or updated [AP] (Ch 2, "User and technical documentation").
- *Assurance statement*: a brief description of the assurance performed; it should refer to known limitations and conditions associated with the analysis [AP] (Ch 2, "Assurance statement").

An unboxed example follows: the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero (DESNZ) and the Department for Business and Trade (DBT) have published Modelling Quality Assurance tools and guidance, used across those departments to ensure analysis meets the AQuA Book's standards and to assure users that proportionate quality assurance has been completed [AE] (Ch 2, "Assurance statement", example "Example of publishing quality assurance tools").

### Model, maturity model, multi-use models

"A model is a tool used to study, or understand, a part of the real world." [V] Models often use quantitative methods and theories from statistics, economics or mathematics, with assumptions, to turn input data into numerical estimates. They can be descriptive ("what is?"), predictive ("what might be?") or prescriptive ("what should be done if?") [V] (Ch 2, "Model").

The Quality Assurance Maturity Model is a structured framework for assessing an organisation's capability in applying quality assurance to analysis, from basic awareness to fully embedded, systematic approaches [AP] (Ch 2, "Maturity Model").

Multi-use models are used by more than one user or group for related but different purposes, and are often complex and large. A Steering Group may be created to oversee them; it should be chaired by the senior officer in charge of the group developing the model and include senior representatives of each major user group, whose members may have decision-making responsibilities in their own areas [AP] (Ch 2, "Multi-use models").

### Quality analysis

"Quality analysis is fit for the purpose it was commissioned to meet." [V] It should be accurate, appropriately assured, evidenced, proportionate to its effect, adequately communicated, documented, and accepted by its commissioners [AP] (Ch 2, "Quality analysis").

### Roles, symbolic proxies, third parties

The book defines four roles: commissioner, analyst, assurer and approver [AP] (Ch 2, "Roles and responsibilities"); Chapter 5 details them.

A symbolic proxy represents data or variables with symbols instead of concrete values, so one can reason about a program's behaviour, and how inputs lead to outputs, without knowing the exact data values [AP] (Ch 2, "Symbolic proxies").

A third party is any individual or group that is not the commissioner or the analyst, for example someone working for a different department, a different function or an outside company [AP] (Ch 2, "Third party").

### Uncertainty

Uncertainties are things not known, in doubt, or whose effect is hard to know, and they can have major consequences for whether a project, programme or analysis meets its objectives. The book points to the National Audit Office's good practice guide on managing uncertainty [AP] [BT]. It notes a common classification into known knowns, known unknowns and unknown unknowns; "The type of uncertainty will influence the analytical approach and assurance activities required." [V] It names the Uncertainty Toolkit for Analysts in Government, produced by a cross-government group, as a tool for assessing and communicating uncertainty [BT] (Ch 2, "Uncertainty").

### Validation, verification, version control

"Validation ensures the analysis meets the needs of its intended users and the intended use environment." [V] (Ch 2, "Validation"). "Verification ensures the analysis meets it specified design requirements." [V] (Ch 2, "Verification"; the source's "it"). Both entries point to *Verification and validation for the AQuA Book* by Paul Glover [BT] (Ch 2, "Validation"; "Verification").

Version control matters so that the latest version of the analysis is used and changes can be seen and quality assured by the assurer; tools and templates can log changes, why and when they were made, and who made them [AP] (Ch 2, "Version control").

## Part IV: Proportionality

### The requirements

> "All analysis shall be assured."
> (Ch 3, "Proportionality")

"The assurer and the analyst shall be independent." [V] The degree of separation depends on factors including the importance of the output and the size and complexity of the analysis. "This does not mean that the analyst should not undertake assurance, rather that there shall also be some formal independent assurance." [V] (Ch 3, "Proportionality"). Assurance should be proportionate to the potential effect and to the size and complexity of the analysis, and "The level of assurance should be guided by a structured assessment of the business risks." [V] (Ch 3, "Proportionality").

### Factors for determining appropriate assurance (Table 3-1)

"While there is a need to be confident in the analysis, it is not necessary to spend months assuring simple analysis that will have a minor influence on a decision." [V] The level of assurance should be appropriate (proportionate) to the analysis, and Table 3-1 lists factors that should be considered [AP] (Ch 3, "3.1 Factors for determining appropriate assurance"). The ten factors and the book's comments:

| Factor | The book's comment |
|---|---|
| Business criticality | Different issues affect how business critical analysis is, for example its financial, legal, operational, political and reputational effects [AP]. |
| Relevance of the analysis to the decision-making process | When analysis is one component of a broad evidence base, less assurance is required for it than if the decision rests heavily on it alone; significant assurance is still likely to be required for the whole evidence base [AP]. |
| Type and complexity of analysis | Highly complex analysis needs more effort to assure and may need appropriate subject matter experts [AP]. |
| Novelty of approach | A previously untried method needs more assurance; confidence grows as the technique is repeatedly tested [AP]. |
| Reusing or repurposing existing work | Reuse may need validation and verification, for example confirming the original method and assumptions data are still appropriate for the new requirement [AP]. |
| Level of precision required in outputs | Lower-precision analysis often uses simplified assumptions, models and data; the assurance approach is the same but takes less time [AP]. |
| Amount of resource available for the analysis and assurance | "The value for money of any additional assurance must be balanced alongside the benefits and risk appetite that exists." [V] Analysis used for many purposes, such as population projections, may need more assurance than any single decision it supports would suggest [AP]. |
| Longevity of the analysis | "Ongoing analysis will require robust change control and regular review." [V] |
| Effects on the public | Analysis with a significant effect on the public may require more assurance [AP]. |
| Repeat runs for the same analysis | "Assurance should concentrate on version control and the assurance of data and parameters for each run." [V] |

(Ch 3, "3.1 Factors for determining appropriate assurance", Table 3-1.) The book points readers to the Data Quality Hub's *Quality Questions and Red Flags* [BT] (Ch 3, "3.1 Factors for determining appropriate assurance").

### Assurance techniques by risk and complexity (Figure 3-1)

Figure 3-1 shows assurance techniques that might be considered for different levels of analysis complexity and business risk. The text description names four: consultation on methods (internal to expert), use of RAP tools (minimal viable to full project), analyst-assurer separation (analyst-led testing to external audit), and documentation detail (in-line to full project) [AP]; "The need for more assurance interventions increases with the complexity of the analysis and the business risk associated with it." [V] (Ch 3, "3.1 Factors for determining appropriate assurance", Figure 3-1 description). The SVG labels its axis "Business Risk and/or Analytical Complexity" from Low to High and its four rows "Consultation on methods/assumptions" (Internal consultation to Expert consultation), "Use of RAP tools" (Minimal viable RAP to Full RAP project), "Analyst-assurer separation" (Analyst-led testing to External audit) and "Documentation detail" (In-line documentation to Full project documentation) [AP] (SVG label, `Figure_3-1_Business_Risk_and_or_Analytical_Complexity_.svg`).

"The interventions in figure 3-1 must not be viewed in isolation. The interventions should build on each other." [V] Complex, risky analysis that would benefit from external review should also use the methods relevant to low risk or complexity, such as analyst-led testing and internal consultation [AP] (Ch 3, "3.1 Factors for determining appropriate assurance"). "The total elimination of risk will never be achieved" [V], so a balance should reduce overall business risk to an acceptable level; the diagram shows a few practical techniques, and the analyst should consider and implement others where necessary [AP] (Ch 3, "3.1 Factors for determining appropriate assurance").

### Structured assessment of business risk (Figure 3-2, Table 3-3)

> "Business risk should be viewed as the combination of the potential effect of analytical errors and the likelihood of errors occurring. In situations where the risk is high, it is more important to reduce likelihood of errors than the level of the effect."
> (Ch 3, "3.2 Structured assessment of business risk and complexity")

The book frames this as a risk matrix that estimates risk for each combination of effect and likelihood. "The effect the analysis will have is usually beyond the control of the analyst to change" [V], so there are few options to lessen the effect, but there will usually be treatments, involving additional assurance, that make the risk less likely to occur [AP] (Ch 3, "3.2 Structured assessment of business risk and complexity"). The text description of Figure 3-2 says likelihood of error rises from left to right, severity of effect rises from bottom to top, and risk rises away from the bottom-left corner, highest in the top-right cells [AP] (Ch 3, "3.2 Structured assessment of business risk and complexity", Figure 3-2 description). The SVG's text layer carries only the axis and title labels "Effect", "Likelihood" and "Risk"; the matrix itself is drawn as unlabelled cells filled in shades of red, so the SVG adds no cell-level wording [AP] (SVG label, `Table_3.2_risk_matrix_v2.svg`).

Where business risk is high, appropriate mitigations "must be considered to reduce the probability of errors occurring" [V], depending on mitigations already in place and on the complexity of the analysis. For simple analysis, review by an appropriate expert may be enough additional mitigation; for complex analysis already using a wide range of internal assurance, options such as external peer review may be necessary [AP] (Ch 3, "3.2 Structured assessment of business risk and complexity"). With significant time and resource constraints it may not be possible to do as much assurance as desirable: "In these situations, addressing the areas of greatest risk should take priority." [V] The commissioner should be told how risks were addressed and what risks remain, with appropriate caveats [AP] (Ch 3, "3.2 Structured assessment of business risk and complexity").

Table 3-3, Responses to risk assessment levels [AP] (Ch 3, "3.2 Structured assessment of business risk and complexity", Table 3-3):

| Assessed risk | Mitigations to consider |
|---|---|
| High | "High risk should not be tolerated." [V] New assurance measures must be considered to treat the likelihood of errors; if treatment is not an option, terminating or transferring the risk must be considered; if the risk must still be tolerated, the commissioner should fully understand it [AP]. |
| Medium | "Medium risk should not be tolerated without the agreement of the commissioner." [V] New assurance measures should be put in place to treat likelihood; continue with planned or existing mitigations [AP]. |
| Low | "Low risk can be tolerated." [V] Continue with existing or planned mitigations; new treatments may also be considered [AP]. |
| Very Low | "Very low risk can be tolerated." [V] Continue with existing or planned mitigations [AP]. |

The book points to the Orange Book for risk management principles and risk control frameworks [BT] (Ch 3, "3.2 Structured assessment of business risk and complexity").

### Externally commissioned work and black-box models

"Proportionate assurance of externally commissioned work is just as important as for internally produced analysis." [V] The commissioner should be fully informed of the business risk, through documented risk assessments supplied with the work and joint risk assessments planned through the project; mitigation options are similar to internal analysis, and the difference lies in making sure the commissioner fully understands the risks and mitigations [AP] (Ch 3, "3.3 Externally commissioned work").

Analysis may increasingly rest on AI or other black-box models. "With these models the need to understand business risk remains and the same structured approach to assessing business risk should be taken." [V] The challenges are ensuring transparency, having a suitable mix of experts, and understanding what mitigations are possible [AP]. The book notes that the Generative AI Framework for HMG highlights assurance in its "Principle 10" [BT] (Ch 3, "3.4 Black-box models and business risk").

## Part V: Quality assurance culture

### Why culture, and for whom

"Creating and maintaining a strong culture of quality assurance is vital for ensuring analysis is robust and of a high quality." [V] The chapter addresses senior leaders in particular, but says everyone has a role and the approaches are useful for everyone [AP] (Ch 4, "Quality assurance culture"). Culture is "defined as the shared ways of working, beliefs and habits of an organisation" [V]; a strong quality assurance culture means quality assurance "is understood, expected and valued by all those involved in the analytical process" [V], including commissioners, analysts, users, managers, senior leaders and stakeholders, and it also enables effective risk management [AP] (Ch 4, "Quality assurance culture").

A box describes the Department for Education's Quality Assurance Maturity Model: an objective self-assessment method for an organisation's relative strengths and weaknesses, in which organisations judge their QA maturity across nine assessment areas, usable as an aid to setting direction and activities [AE] (Ch 4, "Assessing and Guiding Organisational Performance").

### Leadership

"A strong quality assurance culture starts with senior leaders." [V] They are accountable for the quality of analysis in their departments and should set out the priority of quality and create processes for embedding quality assurance [AP] (Ch 4, "4.1 Leadership"). Annex 4.2 of *Managing Public Money* assigns accountability for appropriate assurance processes to the accounting officer, who may in practice assign it to a senior leader reporting to the senior management board; they may report on the state of assurance in the annual report, as DESNZ does in each annual report [BT] [AE] (Ch 4, "4.1 Leadership").

Senior leaders should ensure clear messaging and standards through guidance, training and regular updates, can show the importance of quality assurance through long-term initiatives such as setting up processes and creating supporting roles and teams, and should ensure teams share an understanding of the quality standards and talk regularly about quality, highlighting successes [AP]. They should empower everyone in the analytical process to identify risks to quality and raise concerns at any level; teams should be able to challenge each other constructively when standards are not met. The Maturity Model calls this the Departmental Governance assessment area [AP] (Ch 4, "4.1 Leadership"). Transparency at all levels (peer review, open source code where possible, external publication of models or methods, and publishing the Business Critical Analysis register) can help embed the culture [AP]. Senior leaders should also develop processes that let teams report when things have gone wrong, be open and honest, review failures in the assurance process, and share lessons across the analytical community [AP] (Ch 4, "4.1 Leadership").

A box gives a worked case: when the Department for Education made an error in producing the schools national funding formula allocations for 2024-25, it ran a detailed internal review of what went wrong and why quality assurance did not catch it, and commissioned and published an external independent review, which "praised the team for its culture of open learning taking responsibility for mistakes" [V] [AE] (Ch 4, "An open culture when things go wrong").

### Capacity and capability

Senior leaders should ensure staff have enough time for all stages of the life cycle, including design, quality assurance and documentation, and that staff can draw on others' expertise and have the tools and data they need [AP] (Ch 4, "4.2 Capacity and capability").

*Capacity.* Work and time pressures could affect quality; senior leaders can mitigate this through strong prioritisation and by supporting teams to push back on lower-value work, and by ensuring all parties consider quality assurance at every stage [AP]. "If time constraints mean insufficient assurance has taken place this should be explicitly acknowledged and reported in an assurance statement that sets out the known limitations and conditions associated with the analysis." [V] "Peer review should be carried out by independent, skilled and competent individuals or groups." [V] Ways to support independent review may include specific review and audit teams, assurance networks, partnering with another department, or procuring review from the Government Actuary's Department, an academic institution or a contractor; team leaders can make time for peer review and make clear it is part of analysts' roles [AP] (Ch 4, "4.2.1 Capacity"). A box describes HMRC's small analytical team that independently reviews analysis across the department, including a sample of business-critical models, giving assurance for high-profile analysis and sharing best practice [AE] (Ch 4, "HM Revenue and Customs (HMRC) independent review team").

*Capability.* Lack of skills or experience is a risk of error; senior leaders can identify common gaps and provide training or mentoring, and processes for knowledge sharing, innovation and spreading best practice, plus training on departmental assurance processes, help mitigate it [AP]. The Analysis Function's *Advice for policy professionals using statistics and analysis* is named as a resource for commissioners and users [BT] (Ch 4, "4.2.2 Capability").

*Quality assurance champions.* In organisations with a large analytical community, appointing a quality assurance champion or group of champions is called good practice; they may share best practice and advise on issues such as proportionality and communicating assurance [AP] (Ch 4, "4.2.3 Quality assurance champions"). Two boxes give examples: DESNZ's programme of quality assurance colleges, open across government, which uses "a purposefully sabotaged model" [V] to introduce the quality assurance logbook and the department's system of monitoring models through logbooks, with participants joining the Modelling Integrity Network to provide assuring-analyst capacity [AE] (Ch 4, "Building assurance capability"); and HMRC's Quality Champions network, which discusses QA initiatives, quality issues and their resolution, and shares best practice [AE] (Ch 4, "Sharing best practice on quality assurance").

### Tools, data, uncertainty

Out-of-date technology or tools mean analysts cannot follow best practice or must spend time fixing processing issues instead of concentrating on quality; senior leaders can fund new or improved tools, gather common issues and escalate them [AP] (Ch 4, "4.3 Tools"). Data quality and data understanding are a risk to analysis quality; senior leaders can escalate data quality issues with wider data teams and champion changes [AP] (Ch 4, "4.4 Data").

"Uncertainty is an inevitable part of government work." [V] Senior leaders are responsible for a culture in which proportionate handling of uncertainty is part of all analytical work, and should understand how to identify, analyse and plan for uncertainty. The National Audit Office has published guidance for decision makers and senior leaders on managing uncertainty [BT]. "It is the responsibility of decision makers to challenge analysts, as well as other members of a project team, on whether uncertainties have been considered, treated appropriately and communicated." [V] (Ch 4, "4.5 Uncertainty in analysis").

### Governance, transparency and external commissioning

The Government Functional Standard for Analysis sets out the requirements for a governance framework for analysis [BT]. "Each organisation should have a defined and established approach to assurance." [V] It should be applied proportionately to the risk and value of the activity and integrated with the organisation's overall assurance framework [AP] (Ch 4, "4.6 Governance and control"). Project-level governance lets the approver ensure the analysis is fit for purpose; formally agreeing assumptions, which may be recorded in an assumptions log, reduces rework and frees time for assurance. Analytical governance boards for new, high-profile or complex analysis let senior analytical leaders and experts oversee, challenge and spread good practice, and help apply standards equally across similar work [AP] (Ch 4, "4.6 Governance and control").

Transparency at all levels, for example peer review, sharing lessons learnt and making analysis open where appropriate, can contribute to an open culture of high quality work [AP] (Ch 4, "4.7 Transparency").

Analysis may be commissioned externally. "The commissioning department remains accountable for ensuring the requirements set out in the AQuA Book are met when working with third parties" [V] such as arm's length bodies (executive agencies, non-departmental public bodies and non-ministerial departments). A third party may take only the analyst role in the analysis phase, or the analyst, assurer and approver roles in every stage; third parties may set out in a framework document how they will show compliance with Annex 4.2 of *Managing Public Money* and the Analysis Function Standard [AP] (Ch 4, "4.8 Externally commissioned analysis").

## Part VI: Roles and the analytical lifecycle

### Projects as roles and stages

"An analytical project can be viewed as a variation on an archetypal project defined by roles and stages." [V] Chapter 5 gives the overview; chapters 6 to 9 detail each stage and each role's responsibilities in it [AP] (Ch 5, "Roles and the analytical lifecycle").

### The four roles

Organisations may use their own titles. Each role may be filled by a team or committee, but "a single individual (for example, the chair of a committee) will have overall accountability for each role" [V] (Ch 5, "5.1 Roles and responsibilities").

- *Commissioner* (may be known as customer): requests the analysis and sets out requirements; agrees that what the analyst will do will meet the need; accepts the analysis and assurance as fit for purpose [AP].
- *Analyst*: designs the approach, including the assurance, to meet the commissioner's requirements; agrees it with the commissioner; carries out the analysis and their own assurance; acts on the assurer's findings; can be a group, in which case the lead analyst is responsible [AP].
- *Assurer* (may be known as the analytical assurer or assuring analyst): reviews the analyst's assurance; carries out further validation and verification as they see fit; reports errors and areas for improvement to the analyst; undertakes repeated reviews as required; confirms to the approver that the work has been appropriately scoped, executed, validated, verified and documented; can be a group, led by a responsible leader; and "must be independent from the analysts" [V].
- *Approver* (may be known as senior analyst or senior responsible officer): scrutinises the work of analyst and assurer, and confirms (if necessary) to analyst, assurer and commissioner that the work has been appropriately assured [AP].

(Ch 5, "5.1 Roles and responsibilities".)

> "The roles of analyst and assurer shall be distinct from each other. The analyst should carry out their own assurance but responsibility for formal assurance to the approver and commissioner lies with the assurer."
> (Ch 5, "5.1 Roles and responsibilities")

For quick or simple analysis one person may hold more than one role, "apart from the assurer and analyst roles which shall be separate from one another in all cases" [V] (Ch 5, "5.1 Roles and responsibilities").

### The lifecycle

Quality assurance activities should take place throughout a project. An effective process involves ongoing engagement between commissioner and analyst to keep a balance between time, resource and quality and a shared understanding of the assurance needed and risks involved [AP] (Ch 5, "5.2 The analytical lifecycle"). Figure 2, the analytical cycle, is adapted from the Government Functional Standard for Analysis [BT]; quality assurance should take place in every phase and consider proportionality, though considerations may vary with project governance and phase. "All projects will involve some element of every phase of the cycle, even if this is not clearly defined." [V] Transparency about decisions, process, limitations and changes at each stage should be shown in documentation of the analysis, assumptions and data, records of decisions, and records of quality assurance processes and checks [AP] (Ch 5, "5.2 The analytical lifecycle").

- *Engagement and scoping.* Projects typically start with customer engagement, though other events may trigger them. Scoping ensures a common understanding of the problem and aligns expectations with what can be produced; the commissioner communicates the questions and works with the analyst to define requirements and scope. In multi-cycle work this phase may follow delivery and focus on the next stage's questions; research, evaluation and similar projects may need more effort here to gather a wider range of perspectives [AP] (Ch 5, "5.2.1 Engagement and scoping").
- *Design.* The analyst converts the commission into an analytical plan that sets out the assurance required and ensures the analysis can answer the questions; the phase includes communicating and approving plans, and some iteration with the commissioner is to be expected. Larger or multi-cycle projects may stage the work, and plans that depend on earlier insights may be high-level and need a return to design later [AP] (Ch 5, "5.2.2 Design").
- *Analysis.* Planned analysis is undertaken and progress and relevance are monitored; design and plan may be amended for changing circumstances or limitations, records of analysis, changes, decisions and assumptions are kept, and scoping or design may need revisiting. "Throughout this phase traceable documentation of the assurance activities that have been undertaken shall also be produced." [V] In larger projects outputs may complete at different times and other phases may run concurrently [AP] (Ch 5, "5.2.3 Analysis").
- *Delivery, communication and sign-off.* Insights and assurances are communicated to approver and commissioner, well enough for them to judge whether the work has been appropriately assured and meets their requirements; further analysis and assurance may be needed. Activities may include summary packs, reports, dashboards, websites and presentations. Sign-off formally approves results for dissemination and includes confirming the commission was met, documentation and evidence captured, and appropriate assurance conducted; approval may be phased [AP] (Ch 5, "5.2.4 Delivery, communication and sign-off").

### Maintenance and continuous review

"The analytical lifecycle is not a linear process." [V] Where analysis is used on an ongoing basis, all aspects of the lifecycle should be regularly updated, for example checking whether inputs remain appropriate, whether the original communication methods are still best, whether relied-on software is still supported and up to date, and whether the model is still calibrated appropriately, which the book calls particularly important for black box models [AP]. A robust version control process should be in place so changes are appropriately assured [AP] (Ch 5, "5.3 Maintenance and continuous review").

### Urgent analysis

Sometimes urgent analysis cannot follow every step in the guide, for example where "the need for the analysis may outweigh the risk of poor quality" [V]; analysts should then follow the Government Data Quality Hub's *Urgent data quality assurance guidance* [BT] (Ch 5, "5.4 Urgent analysis").

## Part VII: Engagement and scoping

### Purpose of the stage

In the first stage the commissioner's requirements are scoped and the stage identifies what is relevant. "During this engagement and scoping stage the commissioner and the analyst shape the analysis by developing a shared understanding of the problem and the context." [V] That shared understanding is the basis for designing analysis that meets the requirements [AP] (Ch 6, "Engagement and scoping").

### Responsibilities

- *Commissioner* should inform the analyst of important aspects of the problem, scope, constraints and issues; be available to shape the work; understand the risks where time and resource pressures constrain the approach; share any sources of uncertainty identified; sign off the analyst's specification document; and, if possible, indicate the consequences for decision-making of different degrees of uncertainty, which may let the analyst work at a proportionate level [AP] (Ch 6, "6.1.1 The commissioner’s responsibilities").
- *Analyst* should engage with the commissioner to identify the question, context, boundaries, constraints (such as deadlines and available resource), assumptions, risks, identified uncertainties and business-criticality, and create a specification document capturing the commissioner's requirements. The specification should define scope and constraints, and "It should state the acceptable level of risk and the required level of assurance." [V] It may also state the degree of uncertainty allowed for decision-making and record identified sources of uncertainty; the analyst should share it with the commissioner for sign-off [AP] (Ch 6, "6.1.2 The analyst’s responsibilities").
- *Assurer* may confirm that engagement has been sufficient to understand the problem, and for more business critical projects may wish to confirm that the specification captures the outcomes of engagement [AP] (Ch 6, "6.1.3 The assurer’s responsibilities").
- *Approver* should note the new project and confirm resources and plans are in place for appropriate assurance, for example making sure analyst and assurer know local assurance protocols, and might help secure a qualified and experienced assurer. The approver should ensure enough governance supports the analyst, particularly where analysis supports business critical decisions; this may need revisiting at design if a novel or riskier approach is required, for example AI models [AP] (Ch 6, "6.1.4 The approver’s responsibilities").

### Assurance activities

If the commissioner cannot present a well-defined problem, engagement may require problem structuring methods; the Strategic Choice Approach, Rich Pictures and Systems Thinking are named as techniques to reach joint understanding and define scope, with a pointer to the Systems Thinking Toolkit [BT] (Ch 6, "6.2 Assurance activities"). For complex engagement techniques or business critical projects, the assurer might also assure the engagement methodology [AP]. The stage should lead to agreement on the outputs, "including acceptable levels of accuracy, precision and margins of error" [V], which informs the handling and assurance of uncertainty later. The commissioner should pass on relevant information about data sources and data quality, and analyst and commissioner should clarify risks and effects on outcomes to inform proportionate assurance, and agree resource and timeline constraints [AP] (Ch 6, "6.2 Assurance activities").

### Documentation, uncertainty, black box and multi-use models

The output should be a specification document capturing the joint understanding of the task. It provides a reference for later validation (confirming the analysis meets the specification) and gives the approver evidence at delivery; it should be signed off by the commissioner and might also be reviewed by the assurer [AP] (Ch 6, "6.3 Documentation").

The stage informs the treatment of uncertainty by providing a clear definition of the analytical question, identifying sources of high or intractable uncertainty, and establishing how the analysis will inform decisions [AP] (Ch 6, "6.4 Treatment of uncertainty").

Where black box models such as AI or machine learning are to be delivered, the stage "should include discussions around ethics and risks to assess whether such models would be appropriate for addressing the given problem" [V]; such discussions might cover regulation such as UK GDPR, organisational skills, internal governance, regular tests that the model still works as expected, and risk management [AP] (Ch 6, "6.5 Black box models").

With multi-use models the analyst may need to engage a group of end-users; where requirements differ or contradict, techniques such as Strategic Options Development and Analysis (SODA) and Soft Systems Methodology may be used to build a shared understanding [AP] [BT] (Ch 6, "6.6 Multi-use models").

## Part VIII: Design

### The analytical plan

In design, the analyst creates an actionable analytical plan from the agreed scope [AP] (Ch 7, "Design"). The plan's development should consider: methodology, including the treatment of uncertainty; project management approach (for example Agile Software Development, Waterfall planning, or a combination); sourcing of inputs and assumptions; data and file management; change management and version control; programming language and software; code management, documentation and testing; communication between stakeholders; verification and validation procedures across the project; documentation to be delivered; the process for updating the plan; the process for ongoing review and maintenance of models, including inputs, calibrations and continued support for relied-on software; ethics; reporting; and the use and application of the analysis [AP] (Ch 7, "Design"). "Iteration of the plan between the commissioner and the analyst is normal and expected while the analytical design develops." [V] (Ch 7, "Design").

### Reproducible analytical pipelines

A box names a Reproducible Analytical Pipeline (RAP) as the recommended approach for developing analysis in code, and states that RAPs shall follow the practices in the Analysis Function's *Quality Assurance of Code for Analysis and Research* manual and shall meet the requirements of the RAP minimum viable product [AP] [BT] (Ch 7, "Reproducible analytical pipelines").

### Responsibilities

- *Commissioner* should confirm the approach will meet their needs and may review the plan; their expertise can help, for example on input assumptions, data requirements and effective presentation of outputs [AP] (Ch 7, "7.1.1 The commissioner’s responsibilities").
- *Analyst* should develop the method and plan; establish assurance requirements; develop a plan for proportionate verification and validation as described in the National Audit Office *Framework to review models* [BT]; plan in enough time for assurance; document the plan proportionately; and follow organisational governance for project design [AP] (Ch 7, "7.1.2 The analyst’s responsibilities").
- *Assurer* should review the plan to ensure it can carry out the required assurance, may give feedback, and should plan enough time for the assurance activity [AP] (Ch 7, "7.1.3 The assurer’s responsibilities").
- *Approver* may not be heavily involved in smaller projects; for business critical analysis may want to confirm organisational design governance has been followed [AP] (Ch 7, "7.1.4 The approver’s responsibilities").

### Assurance, documentation and uncertainty in design

By the end of design the assurer should know the quality assurance tasks required of them and have assured the necessary elements of the plan. Design assurance should consider whether the plan is likely to address the commissioner's requirements (validation), deliver as intended (verification), and meet the principles of RIGOUR, for example through a well-structured, data-driven plan with a sound design [AP]. For more complex analysis it is called good practice to engage subject matter experts for independent assurance and to understand the accuracy and limitations of the chosen methods, "ideally with tests baselining their response against independent reference cases" [V] (Ch 7, "7.2 Assurance activities").

The design should be documented proportionately; the analyst should produce a design document recording the plan, signed off by the commissioner and possibly reviewed by the assurer. For modelling, an initial model map of data flows and transformations may be produced and updated through the analysis stage. "It is best practice to use formal version control to track changes in the design document." [V] (Ch 7, "7.3 Documentation").

Analysts "should mine the planned analysis systematically for possible sources and types of uncertainty" [V], to maximise the chance of finding all those large enough to breach the acceptable margin of error [AP] (Ch 7, "7.4 Treatment of uncertainty in the design stage").

### Black box models in design

"Using black box models places greater weight on the design of the analysis and the assurance and validation of outputs by domain experts." [V] The government's guidance on AI assurance is cited for design considerations including risk assessment, impact assessment, bias audits and compliance audits [BT] (Ch 7, "7.5 Black box models"). In designing AI and machine learning models, the analyst should define the situation to model and the prediction to make; assess the quality of data that could be used, including data used in any pretrained models; carry out a literature review to identify appropriate modelling and verification methods and document the rationale; and consider the training, validation and testing strategy, where "it is usual to design a model with a fraction of the data, validate with a separate portion and then test the final model with the data that was not used in the design" [V] (Ch 7, "7.5 Black box models"). The analyst should also consider the strategy for testing a pre-trained model, including validation methods such as calculating similarity to labelled images or ground truths for generative AI; automatic checks to flag unexpected behaviour, which the book calls important where the model will be used frequently for regular decisions or deployed into production; a plan for maintenance and continuous review, including thresholds or timelines for retraining and the resources needed; referral to an ethics committee or similar group, with a pointer to the Data Ethics Framework; and a peer or academic review process to test methods and design decisions [AP] (Ch 7, "7.5 Black box models").

### Multi-use models in design

Design should take into account the needs of all users; an Analysis Steering Group may be an effective channel to a range of user groups. Multi-use models may have a modular structure with different analysts and assurers per element, and "The design of assurance activities should capture both the assurance of individual modules and their integration." [V] (Ch 7, "7.6 Multi-use models").

## Part IX: Analysis

### The stage

In the analysis stage, the planned analysis is undertaken and assured, and progress and relevance are monitored; the design may be amended for changing circumstances, emerging information, unexpected difficulties or limitations; the stage includes "maintaining appropriate and traceable records of the analysis and assurance activities conducted, changes, decisions and assumptions made" [V]; and design or scoping may need revisiting [AP] (Ch 8, "Analysis").

### Responsibilities

- *Commissioner* should be available for input and clarification and should review changes in design or methodology the analyst raises [AP] (Ch 8, "8.1.1 The commissioner’s responsibilities").
- *Analyst* should conduct the verification and validation activities designed in the analytical plan (the tape's bullet reads "follow the conduct the verification and validation activities", as does the GOV.UK HTML); provide traceable documentation of the assurance undertaken; respond to and act on the assurer's recommendations as appropriate; proportionately follow best practice for code development where relevant; document the data, as described in the Government Data Quality Framework [BT], and the methods; ensure documentation is sufficient for the assurer; document changes to the plan proportionately; and keep contact with commissioner and assurer so they can say whether the analysis still meets needs or whether there are new requirements [AP] (Ch 8, "8.1.2 The analyst’s responsibilities").
- *Assurer.* "The assurer shall:" [V] review the analyst's assurance; carry out further validation and verification as they see fit; report errors and areas for improvement; and review that the work proportionately adheres to best practice for code development where relevant. The assurer may need to re-review work, give feedback on changes to the plan, and consider whether they are qualified to assure a revised methodology [AP] (Ch 8, "8.1.3 The assurer’s responsibilities").
- *Approver* should know the progress of the analysis and be available to approve at delivery [AP] (Ch 8, "8.1.4 The approver’s responsibilities").

### Verification and validation

Verification that the implemented methodology meets the design requirements should be part of the analysis [AP]. The book cites Whitener and Balci (1989), who reviewed verification techniques for simulation modelling, as techniques that also extend to analysis more broadly [BT]: informal analysis (human reasoning and subjectivity); static analysis (tests of the implementation before it is run, for example code conventions); dynamic analysis (behaviour during execution, including unit, integration and stress testing); symbolic analysis (how inputs are transformed into outputs using symbolic proxies, with techniques like path tracing and cause-effect testing); constraint analysis (the implementation of constraints during model execution, including assertions and boundary analysis); and formal analysis (logical correctness through formal verification such as logic or mathematical proofs) [AP] (Ch 8, "8.2.1 Verification and validation").

"Validation is testing whether the product meets the requirements of users. It is important to involve the users in the process." [V] Methods include quantification and judgement of acceptable sensitivity, specificity, accuracy, precision and reproducibility; validation of models includes testing the validity of the conceptual model and the operational validity of any computerised model [AP] (Ch 8, "8.2.1 Verification and validation"). "The analyst has primary responsibility for conducting verification and validation." [V] The assurer reviews it, conducts or recommends more as required, and may refer to the specification document to assure the analysis meets it [AP] (Ch 8, "8.2.1 Verification and validation").

### Data validity

Testing data validity, for example that data meet the specification they are used for, is called "a vital part of analysis" [V]. Procedures include testing internal consistency, screening for outliers, trends and expected distributions, and assuring robust data management practices such as automating data creation and sourcing [AP]. Consideration may be given to the conditions for data to stay valid; in some cases it may be appropriate to specify a "sunset date" for data, the date beyond which it should be refreshed or reviewed [AP] (Ch 8, "8.2.2 Data validity and data considerations").

"It is rare to have the perfect dataset for an analytical commission." [V] The data may not be available in time, its definition may not align with the commission, there may be data or coverage gaps, or the data may be experimental or otherwise immature [AP]. Where no directly relevant data exist, surrogate data (measurements of another parameter, or of the parameter under different conditions) can often be used; this implies extrapolation and adds uncertainty, which it may be possible to quantify using expert knowledge of the relationship [AP]. The effect of a proxy dataset should be explored; if its uncertainty bears heavily on the analysis its appropriateness should be revisited, and the exploration and the decision to use it should be recorded for the assurer to verify [AP] (Ch 8, "8.2.2 Data validity and data considerations").

### Assurance of code

The book points to *Quality Assurance of Code for Analysis and Research*, "known informally as the Duck Book", for detailed good practice on developing and assuring analytical software, covering structuring code, documentation, version control, data management, testing, peer review and automation [BT] (Ch 8, "8.2.3 Assurance of code"). "The analyst shall follow the guidance for good quality code development in a proportionate manner and the assurer shall review this accordingly." [V] (Ch 8, "8.2.3 Assurance of code").

### Documentation and uncertainty

The analyst should maintain records of the work; fully document code to agreed standards; log the data, assumptions, inputs and decisions; record the verification and validation undertaken, noting outstanding activities, remedial action and its effect; and produce user and technical documentation. For modelling, the analyst may include a model map [AP] (Ch 8, "8.3 Documentation").

Where scoping and design identified and described risks and uncertainties, the analysis stage "assesses and quantifies how uncertainty may influence the analytical outcome" [V] and its contribution to the range and likelihood of outcomes; the Uncertainty Toolkit reviews quantification methods [BT], and analyst and assurer verification and validation should assure the treatment of uncertainty [AP] (Ch 8, "8.4 Treatment of uncertainty").

### Black box and multi-use models in analysis

"Black box models such as AI and machine learning models are not as transparent as traditionally coded models." [V] This adds challenge to assuring them. Three bullets follow with no lead-in sentence in the source: they should include the verification steps set out in design; should include validation and verification of automatic tests that the model behaves as expected; and may include performance testing in a live environment [AP]. The book points to the *Portfolio of AI assurance techniques* and *Introduction to AI Assurance* [BT] (Ch 8, "8.5 Black box models").

In multi-use models, elements may be analysed and edited at different times, which requires mechanisms for assuring that changes integrate into the larger model as expected. "An example of how this can be achieved is by using test suites." [V] (Ch 8, "8.6 Multi-use models").

## Part X: Delivery, communication and sign-off

### The transition the stage marks

"The successful delivery of analysis to the commissioner marks its transition from being a product under development to one that is fit and ready to be used to inform decision-making in your organisation and, possibly, inform the public." [V] (Ch 9, "Delivery, communication and sign-off").

### Responsibilities

- *Commissioner* should confirm the analysis is likely to meet their needs, use it as specified, and understand and apply any limitations [AP] (Ch 9, "9.1.1 The commissioner’s responsibilities").
- *Analyst* shall follow organisational governance for delivery and sign-off, including, where appropriate, updating the business-critical analysis register and making the analysis publicly available, and shall describe any limitations to its use. The analyst should make communication meet audience requirements such as accessibility, and be ready for challenge from the approver or scrutiny from boards; the analyst should communicate the assurance state to the approver if the assurer does not [AP] (Ch 9, "9.1.2 The analyst’s responsibilities").
- *Assurer* should communicate the assurance state to the approver, including confirmation that the work has been appropriately scoped, executed, validated, verified and documented and "provides adequate handling of uncertainty" [V]; the analyst may do this instead [AP] (Ch 9, "9.1.3 The assurer’s responsibilities").
- *Approver* shall review the assurance evidence; be confident that the analysis meets the design requirements, is of sufficient quality and is adequately and proportionately documented; and follow organisational governance for sign-off, including updating the business-critical analysis register where appropriate. The approver should challenge the analysts enough to gain assurance of fitness for purpose and should give the analyst evidence that outputs have been properly reviewed and formally approved [AP] (Ch 9, "9.1.4 The approver’s responsibilities").

### Delivery

The assurer (or analyst) should communicate the assurance state to the approver with evidence of proportionate quality assurance and show the analysis is ready. This may include confirming that it uses suitable data and assumptions; has provision for regular review of whether methodology, data and assumptions remain valid, or a "sunset date", defined here as "a date beyond which the analysis and / or the model should not be used" [V]; meets the purpose of its commission; was carried out correctly and to specification; has a risk assessment and statement against the programme risk register; meets analytical standards such as coding and documentation; adheres to relevant professional codes such as the Code of Practice for Statistics [BT]; and is accompanied by a completed assurance statement where appropriate [AP] (Ch 9, "9.2.1 Delivery"). "Though not strictly assurance" [V], the analyst should also consider security ratings, retention policies, intellectual property, and ethics and related concerns [AP] (Ch 9, "9.2.1 Delivery").

The approver should scrutinise the evidence, approve the work if it meets the required standard, and feed the outcome back to the analyst; the scrutiny should be proportionate to the analysis's likely effect and the governance process, following the principles of proportionality. The commissioner should use the analysis as specified at the start of the cycle, applying the limitations the analyst described [AP] (Ch 9, "9.2.1 Delivery").

### Communication

"Effective and transparent communication is essential to ensure analysis is adopted and trusted by the commissioner and onward users." [V] Audiences may include commissioners and users; external scrutineers such as the Public Accounts Committee, the National Audit Office and internal and external auditors; the public, through publications and Freedom of Information Act requests; academic experts, possibly through a departmental Areas of Research Interest document; and national and international governmental partners [AP] (Ch 9, "9.2.2 Communication"). "The form of communication should be tailored to the audience." [V] Communication should be quality assured proportionately so it reflects the results accurately; the Analysis Function's *Making Analytical Publications Accessible Toolkit* is named for accessibility [AP] [BT]. Published outcomes should follow departmental and statutory guidance: the regulatory guidance for official statistics and national statistics, the Government Social Research Publication protocol, and recommendations from the Evaluation Task Force for evaluations [BT] (Ch 9, "9.2.2 Communication").

### Sign-off

The approval process may vary with the analysis's likely effect, the organisation's approval process, and the nature of the programme, project or board approving it. "The formality of the sign-off process should be governed by organisational procedures and be proportionate to the analysis." [V] The approver should give the analyst evidence of review and formal approval, for example the notes of the board where the approval decision was made [AP] (Ch 9, "9.2.3 Sign-off").

### Documentation at handover

When analyst and assurer are satisfied the analysis is ready, they should ensure its supporting documentation is ready and has also been quality assured. It may include specification and design documentation; logs of data, assumptions and decisions with source, ownership, reliability and any sensitivity analysis; user and technical documentation; advice on uncertainty and its effect on outputs; a description of the limits of the analysis and what it can and cannot be used for; presentation materials; a record of methods, dependencies, process maps, change and version control logs and error reporting; the code-base where open publication is agreed; the test plan and test results; a statement of assurance; and a statement that ethical concerns have been addressed, especially where black-box models are applied [AP] (Ch 9, "9.3 Documentation").

### Uncertainty

The book lists government guidance on presenting and communicating uncertainty when describing the limits of use: the Office for Statistical Regulation's *Approaches to presenting uncertainty in the statistical system*, the Uncertainty Toolkit for Analysts, and the Analysis Function note *Communicating quality, uncertainty and change* [BT] (Ch 9, "9.4 Treatment of uncertainty").

### Black-box models at sign-off

The approver is responsible for signing off that all risks and ethical considerations around black-box models have been addressed, with reference to the principles of the *Artificial Intelligence Playbook for the UK Government* [AP] [BT]. This may include formal consultation and approval by an ethics committee or similar, provision for regular review (including whether ongoing peer review is needed to keep up with the latest guidance and assurance methods), and communicating the model's "health" to the commissioner at regular intervals [AP] (Ch 9, "9.5 Black-box models and the delivery, communication and sign-off stage"). A box explains: "Model effectiveness can change over time." [V] A model may suffer data drift, with performance falling when it is trained on historical data but used in production on current data, because it "is no longer conditioned on the current state of the data" [V] (Ch 9, "Regularly reviewing model health").

### Multi-use models at delivery

"There is a greater risk that multi-use models may be used for purposes outside the intended scope." [V] So it is important that the analyst very clearly communicates limitations and intended use to all users, and the analyst may consider testing communication with different user groups [AP] (Ch 9, "9.6 Multi-use models").

### Analytical transparency

"Supporting and encouraging the public to understand and scrutinise analysis promotes public confidence in decisions." [V] This includes informing the public about models used for business-critical decisions, making analysis open and ensuring transparency; the UK Statistics Authority's guidance on applying the Code of Practice for Statistics principles of Trustworthiness, Quality and Value to models is cited [BT] (Ch 9, "9.7 Analytical transparency").

*Business critical models register.* Departments and arm's length bodies should publish a list of business critical models (BCM) in use "at least annually" [V], meeting accessibility guidelines. Each should decide what counts as business critical by influence on significant financial and funding decisions, necessity to a departmental business plan, or where an error could cause serious financial, legal or reputational damage; definitions and thresholds should align with the organisation's risk framework; the thresholds should be agreed by the director of analysis or equivalent [AP]. Arm's length bodies publish their own list unless agreed otherwise, with their accounting officer accountable and the sponsor department's accounting officer overseeing [AP]. The list should include all business critical models unless an internally documented, director-agreed reason excludes one. Justifications may include, but are not limited to, Freedom of Information Act 2000 exemptions, national security, policy under development and commercial interests; further reasons may apply where the risk of a negative consequence outweighs the benefits of publication, "For example, where population behaviour may change in response to awareness of a model or modelling." [V] Entries should give the name of the analysis or model and its use, with links to published material [AP] (Ch 9, "9.7.1 Business critical models register").

*Open publishing of analysis.* To support public scrutiny, departments may choose to open the analysis or model (for example source code or spreadsheets) with relevant data, assumptions, methodology and outputs; open publishing of source code lets others reuse and build on the work [AP]. The guidance for publishing business critical lists should be applied, since publication may sometimes be inappropriate; "if the analysis is extremely complex it may be more appropriate to publish summary information to make the analysis more accessible" [V] (Ch 9, "9.7.2 Open publishing of analysis").

## Part XI: Resources and closing matter

### Written resources

The key additional resources are the Government Functional Standard for Analysis, the Green Book, the Magenta Book and the Orange Book [BT] (Ch 10, "10.1 Written resources"). For performing analysis: the Uncertainty Toolkit for Analysts in Government; *Advice for policy professionals using statistics and analysis*; the Data Ethics Framework; the Government Data Quality Framework; and the Reproducible Analytical Pipelines guidance [BT] (Ch 10, "10.1.1 Guidance and advice for performing analysis"). For performing assurance: the Department for Education's Quality Assurance Maturity Model; the National Audit Office *Framework to review models*, described as a structured approach to judge whether modelling outputs "are reasonable, robust and have a minimal likelihood of errors being made" [V]; DESNZ modelling tools and QA guidance, including for models developed by third parties; *Introduction to AI assurance*; and the Duck Book [BT] (Ch 10, "10.1.2 Guidance and advice for performing assurance"). For communicating analysis: the OSR's *Approaches to presenting uncertainty in the statistical system*; *Communicating quality, uncertainty and change*; the *Making Analytical Publications Accessible Toolkit*; and three directions in modal form: if publishing statistics "you shall follow your organisation’s guidance" [V] and the regulatory guidance for official and national statistics; if publishing research, you shall follow organisational guidance and the Government Social Research Publication protocol; if publishing an evaluation, refer to the Evaluation Task Force's recommendations [AP] (Ch 10, "10.1.3 Guidance and advice for communicating analysis").

### External sources of quality assurance

The Government Actuary's Department "can provide expert quality assurance reviews of models across the public sector" [V]; the book describes GAD as financial risk professionals expert in reviewing models on modern platforms including Excel, R and Python, and says "As a non-ministerial department, GAD can offer unique support from within government." [V] (Ch 10, "10.2 External sources of quality assurance").

### Improving the book

"The AQuA Book, when final, will comply with the www.gov.uk accessibility statement." [V] Compliance does not extend to third-party content outside www.gov.uk referenced from the guidance [AP] ("Improving the book", "Accessibility"). The book invites comments and suggestions by email to the Analysis Function, with "AQuA Book" in the subject line [AP] ("Improving the book", "Help us improve this book").
